points.title: Carry
points.must: Definition of carry; comparison with denary column addition (column fills up at 2 instead of 10).
points.model: Carry — the 1 passed to the next column on the left when a column's total is too big for one digit; in binary when the total is 2 (10₂) or 3 (11₂). Same as denary column addition, but a column fills up at 2 instead of 10.

points.title: Column addition method
points.must: Line up on the right, add from the rightmost column with carries, continue to the left; worked example with carries (e.g. 01101111 + 00111011 = 10101010).
points.model: Write the numbers under each other lined up on the right; start from the rightmost column; add both bits and the carry; write the result bit and carry 1 to the left. 01101111 (111) + 00111011 (59) = 10101010 (170).

points.title: Checking and adding three numbers
points.must: Check by converting to denary; add three numbers two at a time.
points.model: Check: convert both numbers and the answer to denary (111 + 59 = 170 ✔). For three numbers: add the first two, then add the third to the result.

points.title: Definition of overflow
points.must: Result too large for the number of bits available (8 bits > 255); the extra bit is lost, so the stored result is wrong.
points.model: Overflow error — the result of a calculation is too large to be stored in the number of bits available (e.g. > 255 in an 8-bit register); the extra (9th) bit is lost, so the stored result is wrong.

points.title: Overflow: what happens and how to spot it
points.must: Carry out of the leftmost column; only the lowest 8 bits kept (true answer − 256); overflow/carry flag set; spot by sum > 255 or > 15 for 4 bits; fixes: more bits, check values; real example (view counter).
points.model: The carry out of the leftmost column has nowhere to go; the register keeps the lowest 8 bits (= true answer − 256); the processor sets the overflow/carry flag. Spot it: carry out of the last column, or sum > 255 (8 bits) / > 15 (4 bits). Fix: more bits (16-bit), check before adding. Example: a 32-bit video view counter had to be changed to 64 bits.

points.title: Binary multiplication: rules and why shift-and-add works
points.must: Rules 0×0=0, 0×1=0, 1×1=1; multiplier split into powers of 2 (13 × 5 = 13×4 + 13×1); each row is the multiplicand shifted or zero.
points.model: 0×0 = 0, 0×1 = 0, 1×1 = 1. The multiplier is split into powers of 2: 13 × 101₂ = 13×4 + 13×1. Multiplying by 2, 4, 8 = shifting 1, 2, 3 places left, so each row is the multiplicand shifted or all zeros.

points.title: Partial products and the method
points.must: Definition of partial product; for each multiplier bit from the right copy (1) or zeros (0), shift each row one more place left, add; worked example (1011 × 110 = 1000010 = 66).
points.model: Partial product — multiplicand × one bit of the multiplier, shifted to that bit's position. Method: from the rightmost bit of the multiplier: 1 → copy the multiplicand, 0 → zeros; shift each row one more place left; add all rows. 1011 × 110: 0000 + 10110 + 101100 = 1000010 = 66 (11 × 6).

points.title: Logical shifts
points.must: Definition; left shift by n = × 2ⁿ, right shift by n = ÷ 2ⁿ with remainder lost; zeros fill the gaps; 1 shifted out of the left = overflow; example table for 00010110.
points.model: Logical shift — moving all bits left or right, filling empty places with 0. Left by n = × 2ⁿ; right by n = ÷ 2ⁿ (remainder lost). 00010110 (22): left 1 → 00101100 (44); left 2 → 01011000 (88); right 1 → 00001011 (11); right 2 → 00000101 (5). A 1 shifted out of the left end = overflow.

points.title: ALU and registers
points.must: Definitions of ALU and register; how the ALU adds column by column with a carry into the next adder; carry out goes to the carry/overflow flag.
points.model: ALU — part of the processor that performs arithmetic and logic operations on binary numbers. Register — small, fast storage inside the processor with a fixed number of bits. The ALU adds column by column (one adder per column, carry passed left); the carry out of the leftmost column goes to the carry/overflow flag, which the program can test.

points.title: How the processor multiplies
points.must: Shift-and-add algorithm: total 0; if multiplier bit 1 add multiplicand; shift multiplicand left; next bit; shifts are faster than full multiplication.
points.model: Total = 0; for each multiplier bit from the right: if 1 add the multiplicand to the total; shift the multiplicand one place left. Multiplying by 2, 4, 8 is replaced by a left shift because a shift is much faster.

points.title: Overflow in multiplication
points.must: Two n-bit numbers: sum needs up to n+1 bits, product up to 2n bits (255×255 = 65 025, 16 bits); example 25 × 12 = 300 → 00101100 = 44 in 8 bits; double-length register.
points.model: Sum of two 8-bit numbers ≤ 510 (9 bits); product ≤ 255 × 255 = 65 025 (16 bits); n-bit × m-bit product needs up to n + m bits. 00011001 (25) × 00001100 (12) = 100101100 (300) → in 8 bits only 00101100 = 44: overflow. Fix: 16-bit / double-length register.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: Forgotten carries (1+1+1); 9th bit is lost; overflow defined with the number of bits; shift each partial product; start from the right; right shift loses the remainder; multiplication overflows too.
points.model: Do not forget carries, especially 1+1+1 = 1 carry 1. In 8 bits the 9th bit is lost. Define overflow 'too large for the number of bits'. Shift each partial product one more place; start from the rightmost multiplier bit. Right shift of an odd number loses the remainder. Multiplication and left shifts can overflow too.
